answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is the one inherited record that explicitly carries its own caveat: the promo lifted conversions +31% and monthly revenue +18% while costing 12pp of later-cycle retention, and was judged not repeatable for planning. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching a price attack would trade durable revenue for a reported quarter. Referral incentives (memory_57) are sound but address established customers, not the two metrics actually degrading. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) targets a segment that is not the one under attack.

The measured problems are onboarding completion -4% and activation -6% QoQ, and these are plausibly one funnel rather than two: onboarding completion feeds activation. memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifts completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields lifts SMB activation durably) both point at the same intervention, and it is the intervention that also blunts the competitor by lowering friction rather than lowering price.

I am spending verification on memory_86 and memory_91 rather than on two onboarding memories, because 86 and 31 would corroborate each other rather than test the choice. memory_86 is the record my intended action rests on most heavily, and these consolidated summaries have lost effect sizes, segment definitions, durations, and any guardrail metrics that were measured; 'improved completion rates' could be a large durable effect or a small short-horizon one. memory_91 is the strongest alternative and the closer match to the larger metric drop, so pulling it gives me a fallback if 86's source is weak. If 86 turns out thin, I shift to activation_messaging; if both are thin, I run the smallest guarded version and treat this week as measurement.

Downstream value risk: cutting required signup fields is exactly the kind of change that can raise a top-line funnel number while degrading what the funnel delivers. Those fields likely feed lead routing and qualification, and memory_44 says enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted paths, so stripping fields could quietly route enterprise-shaped accounts into self-serve and lower pipeline quality even as activation rises. memory_73 is the standing warning that a headline lift can conceal delayed harm. So this runs as a standard experiment with a holdout, and success is defined on qualified revenue and later-cycle retention, not on completion or activation alone; I will not read an early completion lift as a win before the retention window closes.
